transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, I... I suppose it's a few things, but there's one thing in particular that really pushed me to make the appointment. I've been feeling just so heavy and down lately, which is hard enough, but... well, I work as a gambling surveillance officer. It's a job that requires a lot of focus, you know? You're staring at screens for hours, looking for the slightest hand movement or anything out of place on the casino floor. And usually, I'm good at it. I have a bachelor's degree, I'm 44, I know how to pay attention. But lately, especially during the really quiet stretches in the surveillance room—like around 3 or 4 in the morning when the floor is mostly empty and it's just me and the monitors—things have been happening. 

What scared me enough to come in is that... I've been hearing voices. And not just faint whispers or people talking in the hallway. I hear them coming right through the monitor speakers. They say these awful things to me. They'll say, "You missed it, Ruth," or, "People are going to get hurt because of you." And the thing is... the terrifying thing is that I know for a fact every single channel is muted. I check them. I double-check them. I even asked my co-worker, Dave, if he heard anything on his shift, or if he heard it when he walked by my station, and he looked at me like I was crazy. He didn't hear a thing. But I hear it so clearly. It's like they're right there, judging me, telling me I'm failing, even when there's no possible way sound should be coming from those speakers. It's just... it's really starting to wear me down, on top of everything else.
Have you ever experienced other strange occurrences, like seeing things that others don’t see, or believing that something is happening that isn’t really there?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I'm not seeing things... well, I guess I should say I'm not seeing things that aren't there. Obviously I'm looking at monitors all night, so I see a lot of things, but they're real things, you know? People playing blackjack, people walking around, the dealers shuffling cards. But no ghosts or shadows or anything strange like that. And I don't... I don't think I believe things that aren't true. I know what's real. I know the speakers are muted, which is why it's so terrifying that I hear the voices. If I believed the speakers were on, I wouldn't be so scared, right? Because then it would just be someone talking on the other end. But I know they're muted. I check the little red light on the console. It's always on when it's muted. I even trace the wire sometimes, just to make sure it's not picking up interference from the radio system we use, because sometimes the walkie-talkies can bleed over, but it's completely separate. So, no, I don't have any weird beliefs or see things. It's just... it's just the voices, and this awful, crushing feeling I have all the time, like everything is just too hard to do anymore. But my eyes are fine. My eyes are the one thing I've always been able to trust in this job.
Have you ever felt that others are plotting against you, or that you have special powers or abilities that others don’t recognize?

No, no, nothing like that at all. I mean, I don't think anyone is plotting against me. My coworkers are fine, mostly. Dave, like I mentioned, he's a good guy, maybe a little lazy on the graveyard shift, but he's certainly not out to get me. And management... well, they just care about the bottom line, making sure nobody is counting cards or skimming chips. They barely know my name, let alone have the time to plot against me. I just sit in my chair, log my reports, and try to make it through to 8 AM. 

And special powers? Oh, definitely not. I mean, I'm good at my job, or at least I used to be before this heaviness set in and the voices started. I have a good eye for detail. I can spot a dealer flashing a hole card from three tables away on a grainy feed, but that's just years of experience and knowing what to look for, not a superpower. It's just training. I went to school, got my degree, and learned how to observe. If I had special powers, I think I'd use them to make myself feel better, you know? To lift this... this weight that makes it so hard to just get out of bed and put my uniform on every night. Or I'd use them to make the speakers stop talking to me when they're muted. 

But no, I'm just a regular person, a 44-year-old woman sitting in a dark room watching other people lose their money. I don't have any grand ideas about myself. In fact, most days lately, I feel like I'm completely worthless, like I can't even do this one job right anymore because I'm so distracted by how awful I feel and those voices telling me I'm missing things. So, no, no plots, no powers. Just me, struggling to get by.

Have there been times when you felt unusually energized, needed less sleep, or felt like your thoughts were racing, where you might have done things that others would consider out of character or excessive?

Energized? Oh, gosh, no. No, if anything, it's the exact opposite. I can't even remember the last time I felt energized. You know, working the graveyard shift—I usually clock in around 10 PM and get out at 6 or maybe 8 AM depending on the rotation—it really messes with your sleep schedule anyway. But even taking the shift work into account, I am just... I'm exhausted all the time. I definitely don't need less sleep. I crave sleep. 

When my shift ends, I drive home, and the sun is usually just coming up, which is honestly a terrible feeling when you feel as heavy as I do. I have these thick blackout curtains in my bedroom, the kind you get at a nice hotel, and I even tape the edges to the wall so no light gets in. I run a box fan just to drown out the neighborhood noise, the garbage trucks and people leaving for their normal jobs. And I'll just lie there. I want to sleep for days. Sometimes I do sleep for ten, twelve hours if I have a day off, but I never, ever wake up feeling refreshed or energized. It’s like I’m moving through molasses from the minute I open my eyes. 

And my thoughts... they definitely don't race. They just sort of... plod along. It takes so much effort just to put a thought together lately, to decide what to eat or even just to get up and brush my teeth before I have to put my uniform back on. I certainly haven't done anything out of character or excessive, unless you count wearing the same sweatpants for three days straight on my weekend because I just didn't have the energy to carry my laundry basket down the hall. I used to be so organized, you know? I kept my apartment spotless, everything in its place. But now... I just don't have the fuel in the tank for any of that. So, no, no bursts of energy or racing thoughts. Just this constant, heavy tiredness that never really goes away, no matter how much I rest.
Have you had a period of time where you felt down or hopeless almost every day for most of the day, and this lasted for at least two weeks in a row?

Two weeks? Oh... oh, doctor, it's been so much longer than two weeks. It feels like it's been months, honestly. Just this endless, unbroken stretch where nothing feels right anymore. It’s every single day. 

Most days, I feel like this heavy, thick gray mood just settles over me before I even get out of bed. Like I was saying earlier about waking up and feeling like I'm moving through molasses... it's exactly that. I'll wake up, and before I even pull the covers back, before my feet even touch the bedroom carpet, I just feel this immense weight. It's almost like a physical pressure on my chest, this grayness that just seeps into everything in my apartment. I'll just lie there staring at the ceiling, dreading the whole process of existing. 

And it doesn't lift, no matter what I do. I manage to drag myself into the shower, put on my uniform—which is this stiff polyester blend that just feels so suffocating and heavy on my shoulders lately—and I drive to work. The drive is... well, the drive is when it really overwhelms me. I take the same route every night, down the interstate, getting off at the exit for the casino. And I can tear up in my car before my shift over nothing more than seeing the casino lights. Just... just seeing those big, bright neon signs against the dark sky, all those flashing colors reflecting off the windshield, knowing I have to go in there and sit in that dark surveillance room... the tears just start coming out of nowhere. 

I'll find myself sitting there in the employee parking structure, gripping the steering wheel with the engine still running, just crying and feeling completely, utterly hopeless about my life. I have to sit there with a tissue and carefully dab my eyes so the shift manager doesn't see that my face is all red and puffy when I clock in. I try to pull myself together, I really do, but it’s just so hard. So, yes, to answer your question, it's every day. Most of the day. It never really goes away, just this constant, heavy gray feeling that I can't shake.
